q: 1. The soil moisture useful for plant growth is .............
explain: Capillary water is held in the soil pores against gravity by surface tension and is the primary source of water that plant roots can actually extract.

q: 2. The field capacity is the moisture content present in the soil .............
options: when all the gravity water is removed from it after saturation
when the oven dry sample absorbs moisture from atmosphere
explain: Field capacity is defined as the amount of soil moisture or water content held in the soil after excess water has drained away by gravity.

q: 3. The field capacity of an irrigation soil depend on .............
options: porosity and depth of root zone
explain: Field capacity is influenced by the total volume of pores (porosity) and how well those pores retain water against gravity (pore size/texture).

q: 4. Available soil moisture is the difference between .............
options: saturation capacity and permanent wilting point
field capacity and permanent wilting point
saturation capacity and temporary wilting point
explain: Available moisture is the range of water held between the Field Capacity (upper limit) and the Permanent Wilting Point (lower limit) that plants can use.

q: 5. The moisture content of the soil below which plants cannot extract sufficient water for their requirements is called .............
explain: At the Permanent Wilting Point, the soil particles hold water so tightly that plants can no longer exert enough suction to extract it, leading to permanent wilting.

q: 6. Soil moisture deficiency is the difference between .............
options: saturation capacity and the existing soil moisture content
field capacity and the existing soil moisture content
permanent wilting point and the existing moisture content
temporary wilting point and the existing moisture content
explain: Soil moisture deficiency represents the amount of water needed to bring the current soil moisture level back up to Field Capacity.

q: 7. The field capacity and dry unit weight of an irrigation soil are 25% and 1.5 g/cc respectively. If the root zone depth is 0.8 m. What is the depth of water required to bring the existing soil moisture of 15% to the field capacity?
explain: Depth = (Dry Wt / Water Wt) * Depth * (FC - MC). Here, $1.5 * 80 * (0.25 - 0.15) = 1.5 * 80 * 0.10 = 12$ cm.

q: 8. The field irrigation requirement is computed as .............
options: net irrigation requirement + field application losses
explain: FIR is the amount of water required to meet the Net Irrigation Requirement (NIR) plus the water lost during application in the field (deep percolation and runoff).

q: 9. The gross irrigation requirement is given by .............
explain: GIR is the total water diverted from the source, covering the Field Irrigation Requirement (FIR) plus losses that occur during transport through canals (conveyance losses).

q: 10. The depth of root zone for rice is generally about .............
explain: Rice has a relatively shallow root system, typically concentrated in the top 12 cm of the soil, though this can vary slightly by variety.

q: 11. The heavy crop among the following is .............
explain: Sugarcane is considered a 'heavy' or perennial crop because it occupies the land for a long duration and requires a high volume of water throughout the year.

q: 12. Identify the correct pair of crop and harvesting time the following .............
explain: Gram is a Rabi crop sown in winter and harvested in spring (March-April).

q: 13. Which of the following is leguminous crop?
explain: Groundnut is a legume, meaning it has the ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through root nodules.

q: 14. What type of crop is the sugarcane?
explain: Sugarcane is a perennial crop because its growth cycle typically spans 10 to 12 months or longer, crossing multiple seasons.

q: 15. The water held in pores of soil by capillary forces against gravity pull is called .............
explain: Capillary water is the water retained in the soil micro-pores by surface tension. It is the only type of soil water available for plant extraction.

q: 16. The laboratory estimate of field capacity is known as .............
explain: Moisture equivalent is the amount of water retained by a saturated soil sample after being subjected to a centrifugal force of 1000 times gravity for 30 minutes, closely approximating field capacity.

q: 17. The ratio of total quantity of water supplied to a crop during its base period to the area is called .............
explain: Delta (Δ) is the total depth of water required by a crop during the entire period the crop is in the field.

q: 18. The area irrigated by one m3/s of water flowing throughout the base period of the crop is called .............
explain: Duty represents the irrigating capacity of a unit of water; it is the area (in hectares) that can be irrigated by a constant discharge of 1 cumec (m3/s).

q: 19. The optimum kor depth for rice is .............
explain: Kor-depth is the depth of the first watering after sowing. Rice, being a water-intensive crop, requires a higher kor-depth of 19 cm compared to other cereals.

q: 20. The optimum kor depth of wheat is .............
explain: Wheat requires less water than rice during its initial growth stage; its standard kor-depth is approximately 13.5 cm (often rounded to 13 cm in exams).

q: 21. Crop rotation means
options: not growing any crop during alternate year
growing simultaneously two different crops in alternate rows
growing different crops in successive seasons
explain: Crop rotation is the practice of growing a series of dissimilar or different types of crops in the same area in sequenced seasons to help restore soil fertility.

q: 22. The duty of well water is more than the duty of canal water because
options: well water is less turbid than canal water
well water is used more economically
well water irrigation incurs less conveyance losses
explain: Duty is higher for wells because the water is closer to the field (less loss) and farmers use it sparingly due to the cost/effort of lifting it.

q: 23. Earthquake forces acting on a gravity dam
options: reduce the self weight of the dam
increase the uplift forces on the base of the dam
increase the horizontal water pressure acting on the dam
explain: Earthquakes generate hydrodynamic pressure (Zanger's formula), which acts as an additional horizontal force against the dam face.

q: 24. Which of the following is also known as superfluous water?
explain: Gravitational water (or superfluous water) is the water that drains out of the soil under the influence of gravity; it is not available for plant use.

q: 25. According to Khosla's potential flow theory, the undermining of the floor commences at
explain: Failure by piping (undermining) begins at the exit point (tail end) of the structure where the exit gradient is maximum.

q: 26. When an oven-dried sample of soil is kept open in the atmosphere, it absorbs some amount of water. This water is known as
explain: Hygroscopic water is the moisture absorbed from the atmosphere by soil particles; it is held very tightly by molecular forces and is unavailable to plants.

q: 27. A part of water which exists in the porous space of the soil by molecular attraction, is known as
explain: Capillary water is held in the soil's small pores against gravity by surface tension; this is the primary source of water for plant roots.

q: 28. Super-fluous water is a also called
explain: Gravitational water is called superfluous because it is in excess of what the soil can hold at field capacity and drains away rapidly.

q: 29. A useful soil moisture for plant growth is
explain: Only capillary water (the moisture between Field Capacity and Wilting Point) can be easily extracted by the root systems of most crops.

q: 30. The amount of water required to fill up the pore spaces in soil particles by replacing all air held in pore spaces, is known as
explain: At saturation capacity, every single pore in the soil is filled with water, and no air remains in the soil matrix.

q: 31. The moisture content of the soil, after free drainage has removed most of the gravity water, is known is
explain: Field capacity represents the maximum amount of water a soil can hold against gravity, usually reached 2–3 days after heavy rain or irrigation.

q: 32. Available moisture may be defined as the
options: moisture content at permanent wilting point
difference in water content of the soil between field capacity and permanent wilting
explain: Available moisture = Field Capacity – Permanent Wilting Point. This is the reservoir of water that plants can actually use.

q: 33. The field capacity of a soil depends upon
explain: Field capacity is influenced by soil texture (porosity) and the ability of the soil to hold water against gravity (capillary tension).

q: 34. Consumptive use of water by a crop is equal to
options: the depth of water consumed by evaporation
the depth of water consumed by transpiration
the depth of water consumed by evaporation and transpiration during crop growth, including water consumed by accompanying weed growth
explain: Consumptive use (Evapotranspiration) includes the water lost from the soil surface and plant leaves, plus the water required for plant metabolic processes.

q: 35. The consumptive use of water of a crop
options: is measured as the volume of water per unit area
is measured as depth of water on irrigated area
may be supplied partly by precipitation and partly by irrigation
explain: Consumptive use is typically expressed as a depth (e.g., mm/day) and can be met by natural rainfall or supplemental irrigation.

q: 36. The ratio between the area of a crop irrigated and the quantity of water required during its entire period of the growth, is known as
explain: Duty represents the relationship between the volume of water and the area of land it can mature. (Hectares per cumec).

q: 37. The total depth of water required by a crop during the entire period the crop is in the field, is known as
explain: Delta ($\Delta$) is the total depth of water (usually in cm or m) required by a crop to come to maturity.

q: 38. The duty is largest
options: at the head of the main canal
at the head of the water course
explain: Duty increases as we move downstream from the canal head toward the field because conveyance losses are reduced as the measuring point gets closer to the crop.

q: 39. The time (in days) that crop takes from the instant of its sowing to that of harvest, is known as ............. period.
explain: Crop period is the actual biological duration from sowing to harvesting, whereas Base period is the duration from the first to the last watering.

q: 40. Crop ratio is the ratio of area irrigated
options: in Rabi season to Kharif season
in Kharif season to Rabi season
under perennial crop to total crop
under perennial crop to non-perennial crop
explain: In irrigation planning, crop ratio is specifically the ratio of the area of Rabi crops to the area of Kharif crops.

q: 41. The duty of irrigation water will be less if
explain: Duty = Area / Discharge. If a crop requires more water (higher discharge), the same volume of water will cover less area, resulting in a lower duty.

q: 42. The relation between duty (D) in hectares/cumec, delta ($\Delta$) in meters and base period (B) in days is
explain: The standard engineering formula derived from volume calculations: $\Delta = (8.64 \times B) / D$.

q: 43. The area in which crop is grown at a particular time or crop season, is called
explain: The correct term for the area actually being cropped at a specific time is 'Net Sown Area' or 'Irrigated Area' during that season (none of the provided options).

q: 44. The first watering before sowing the crop, is known as
explain: Paleo irrigation is the watering done to the dry land before sowing to provide sufficient moisture for germination.

q: 45. The crops require maximum water during
options: first watering before sowing the crops
first watering when the crop has grown a few centimeters
explain: The 'Kor' watering—the first watering after the plant has grown a few centimeters—usually requires the maximum depth of water.

q: 46. The maximum depth in soil strata, in which the crop spreads its root system, and derives water from the soil, is called
explain: Root zone depth determines the reservoir of moisture available to the plant; irrigation is designed to replenish this specific depth.

q: 47. The depth of root zone is 90 cm for
explain: Wheat is typically categorized as having a root zone depth of approximately 90 cm in design calculations.

q: 48. The duty of a crop is 432 hectares per cumec when the base period of the crop is 100 days. The delta for the crop will be
explain: Using $\Delta = 8.64 B/D$: $\Delta = (8.64 \times 100) / 432 = 2$ meters = 200 cm.

q: 49. The average delta of rice crop is nearly
explain: Rice is a water-intensive crop requiring standing water; its total delta usually ranges between 110 cm to 125 cm.

q: 50. The average duty for sugar-cane in hectares/cumec is
explain: Sugar cane is a perennial crop; while it uses a lot of water, its duty is often calculated around 800 hectares/cumec over its long base period.
